### Task 1: Conceptual Questions

#### 1) If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?

If I'm not using a projects environment, I would likely have used a command to set my working directory, such as:

```{r}
setwd("myfolder/homework/")
```

Regardless of projects vs. lose scripts, in order to access the .csv file one level up from the folder I'm currently in, I would use:

```{r}
read.csv(../MyData.csv)  
# This tells R to go backwards one directory ("../"), then find the MyData.csv file.
```

#### 2) What are the major benefits of using R projects?

Using projects saves your workspace state, and makes it possible to skip setting up a working directory. That also makes it more portable to other devices (second computers, etc.).

#### 3) What is Git and what is GitHub?

Git is a version control system to track changes in text files, such as code. GitHub is an online repository of these text files and backups, allowing for easy working between multiple computers and across teams. It can also help track and resolve version control conflicts, such as when two team members are editing the same files.

#### 4) What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?

Tibbles only print the header, instead of the whole data frame, making the output cleaner. Also, similar to other applications (Stata, SAS, SPSS),  modifying a tibble returns a tibble, whereas modifying a data frame usually returns a vector (single variable) that has changed while leaving the rest of the data set behind.

glass_data$TypeOfGlass <- factor(glass_data$TypeOfGlass,
levels = c(1,2,3,4,5,6,7),
labels = c("building_windows_float_processed", "building_
windows_non_float_processed", "vehicle_windows_float_processed", "vehicle_windows_non_float_processed", "containers,", "tableware,", "headlamps"))
glass_data

#### 5) Lastly, add a column to this data set to indicate the wines are white. That is, add a column that has values of ‘white’ for every observation. You can do this via the \$ operator or, if you know it already, the mutate() function from dplyr.

```{r}
wine_data <- wine_data |> mutate(type = "White")
wine_data
```
